'''Sir Ian Lamont Boyd,''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|size=100%|sep=,|FRSE|FRSB|FRS}} (born 9 February 1957) is a Scottish zoologist, environmental and polar scientist, former Chief Scientific Adviser at the [[Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs]] (DEFRA)<ref>'BOYD, Prof. Ian Lamont', Who's Who 2013, A & C Black, an imprint of Bloomsbury Publishing plc, 2013; online edn, Oxford University Press, Dec 2012; online edn, Nov 2012 [http://www.ukwhoswho.com/view/article/oupww/whoswho/U43821 accessed 5 Sept 2013]</ref> and is a professor of biology at the [[University of St Andrews]]. He has been chair of the [[UK Research Integrity Office]] and is president of the [[Royal Society of Biology]].

==Early life and education==
He is son of the zoologist and conservationist [[John Morton Boyd]]. He attended the independent [[George Heriot's School]] in Edinburgh. He went to the [[University of Aberdeen]] from 1975 where he graduated with a [[British undergraduate degree classification#First-class honours|1st class Degree]] in [[Zoology]] in 1979. He subsequently went to [[St John's College, Cambridge]] until 1982 and received a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] degree from [[Cambridge University]] in 1983. He was a [[Winston Churchill Memorial Trusts|Churchill Fellow]] in 1980. He was a pilot in the [[Royal Air Force Volunteer Reserve]] from 1975 to 1978.

==Career==
===Overview===
Boyd's career has evolved from physiological ecologist with the [[Natural Environment Research Council]] [[Institute of Terrestrial Ecology]], to a Science Programme Director with the [[British Antarctic Survey]], Director at the [[Natural Environment Research Council]]'s [[Sea Mammal Research Unit]], Chief Scientist to the Behavioural Response Study for the US-Navy, Director for the Scottish Oceans Institute<ref>{{cite web|url=https://soi.st-andrews.ac.uk/|title=Scottish Oceans Institute - University of St Andrews|website=soi.st-andrews.ac.uk}}</ref> and acting Director and Chairman with the Marine Alliance for Science and Technology for Scotland.<ref name="masts.ac.uk">{{cite web|url=http://www.masts.ac.uk/|title=Marine Alliance for Science and Technology for Scotland (MASTS)|website=Welcome to Marine Alliance for Science and Technology for Scotland (MASTS)}}</ref> He has also been the Chief Executive or board member of several companies including for the [[University of St Andrews]] and Fera Science Ltd. He is currently Professor in Biology at the University of St Andrews and was Chief Scientific Adviser to the [[Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs]] (Defra) from 2012 to 2019. He is also currently on the board of [[UK Research and Innovation]](UKRI) and is co-chair with Scotland's First Minister of the First Minister's Environment Council.

In parallel to his formal positions he has chaired, co-chaired or directed international scientific assessments; his activities focusing upon the management of human impacts on the environment.

He was responsible for establishing the Scottish Oceans Institute at the [[University of St Andrews]] and the Marine Alliance for Science and Technology for Scotland (MASTS),<ref name="masts.ac.uk"/> a cross-institutional research pool including eight of Scotland's universities. As Director of the [[Natural Environment Research Council|NERC]] [[Sea Mammal Research Unit]] he was responsible for providing scientific advice to [[Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs|Defra]] and the [[Scottish Government]] about policies related to marine mammals. He has been a member of the [[Scottish Science Advisory Council]] and is on the Board of Reviewing Editors of [[Science (journal)|Science]]. He was Editor-in-Chief of the Journal of Zoology from 2006 to 2008. He sits on the judging panel for the [[St Andrews Prize for the Environment]].<ref>{{cite web |title=About the St Andrews Prize |url=https://www.st-andrews.ac.uk/st-andrews-prize/about/ |website=st-andrews.ac.uk |publisher=University of St Andrews |access-date=4 March 2023}}</ref>

===DEFRA===
His position as a Director General and Chief Scientific Adviser at [[Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs|Defra]] was announced on 24 April 2012<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.defra.gov.uk/news/2012/04/24/new-chief-scientist-appointed/|title=New Chief Scientist appointed - GOV.UK|website=www.defra.gov.uk}}</ref> and he took up his post on 1 September 2012. In 2017 he announced that he would be leaving Defra after five years as Chief Scientific Adviser but then agreed to stay on following the 2017 General Election when [[Michael Gove]] became the Secretary of State for Defra. He explained in a blog<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ianlboyd.wordpress.com/2017/10/04/opportunities-too-good-to-miss/|title=Opportunities too good to miss|date=4 October 2017|access-date=7 February 2018|archive-date=7 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180207123343/https://ianlboyd.wordpress.com/2017/10/04/opportunities-too-good-to-miss/}}</ref> that Defra ''"is responsible for delivering the basics of life – food, water and air – in sufficient quantities and to a demanding quality standard. As a consequence, we have to deal with some of the most difficult questions facing people and the planet"'' and that ''"like many others, I cannot easily walk away from these challenges and especially when opportunities are opening up which could ratchet us along the track to improvement."''

Since 2011 most government departments have had their own [[Government Chief Scientific Adviser (United Kingdom)|Chief Scientific Adviser]] but Defra has had a Chief Scientific Adviser since its creation in 2001. Predecessors had been Sir [[Howard Dalton]] (2002-2007) and Sir [[Robert Watson (scientist)|Robert Watson]] (2007-2012). Defra was originally formed from the Ministry for Agriculture, Fisheries and Food and part of the Department for the Environment, Transport and the Regions both of which had Chief Scientific Advisers up until the merger.

His appointment was non-political, but he served as scientific adviser to four different Secretaries of State including [[Owen Paterson]], [[Liz Truss]], [[Andrea Leadsom]] and [[Michael Gove]].

===Publications===
====Research====
Boyd has published over 180 peer-reviewed scientific papers (H-index 82), 14 books and has been the author/co-author/editor of several major reports including a marine atlas of Scotland's coastal seas.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gov.scot/Topics/marine/science/atlas|title=Marine Atlas|last=Scottish Government|date=8 December 2009|website=www.gov.scot|access-date=7 February 2018|archive-date=8 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180208004509/http://www.gov.scot/Topics/marine/science/atlas}}</ref> He has been an author of a number of publications about fisheries management both in connection with his native Scotland<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rse.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2016/09/The-Scottish-Fishing-Industry.pdf |title=RSE Inquiry into The Future of the Scottish Fishing Industry|date=March 2004 |website= rse.org.uk|publisher=Royal Society of Edinburgh}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gov.scot/Publications/2010/11/02103454/19|title=The Future of Fisheries Management in Scotland: Report of an Independent Panel|first=St Andrew's House|last=Scottish Government|date=4 November 2010|access-date=7 February 2018|archive-date=8 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180208004446/http://www.gov.scot/Publications/2010/11/02103454/19}}</ref> and globally.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.lenfestocean.org/~/media/legacy/lenfest/pdfs/littlefishbigimpact_revised_12june12.pdf?la=en |title=Little Fish Big Impact|website=lenfestocean.org}}</ref>

His most significant discovery has been the functional relationship between the performance of marine predators and the state of their food supply, first published in a paper in the ''[[Journal of Animal Ecology]]'' in 2001.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1046/j.0021-8790.2001.00534.x |jstor=2693459 |title=Monitoring a marine ecosystem using responses of upper trophic level predators |journal=Journal of Animal Ecology |volume=70 |issue=5 |pages=747–60 |year=2001 |last1=Boyd |first1=I. L |last2=Murray |first2=A. W. A |doi-access=free |bibcode=2001JAnEc..70..747B }}</ref> This suggested that there was likely to be a surplus of marine production which could be exploited by fisheries before there were wider effects on marine ecosystems. Although Boyd had made this discovery in the [[krill]]-based ecosystems of the [[Southern Ocean]], together with colleagues, he showed that this relationship was general for most marine ecosystems. They published a paper in the journal [[Science (journal)|Science]]<ref name=pmid22194577>{{cite journal |doi=10.1126/science.1212928 |pmid=22194577 |title=Global Seabird Response to Forage Fish Depletion--One-Third for the Birds |journal=Science |volume=334 |issue=6063 |pages=1703–6 |year=2011 |last1=Cury |first1=P. M |last2=Boyd |first2=I. L |last3=Bonhommeau |first3=S |last4=Anker-Nilssen |first4=T |last5=Crawford |first5=R. J. M |last6=Furness |first6=R. W |last7=Mills |first7=J. A |last8=Murphy |first8=E. J |last9=Osterblom |first9=H |last10=Paleczny |first10=M |last11=Piatt |first11=J. F |last12=Roux |first12=J.-P |last13=Shannon |first13=L |last14=Sydeman |first14=W. Much of his research has focused on the studying the [[ecological economics]] of marine predators, mostly in Antarctica, and using their energy balances and behavioral and physiological responses to understand the distribution and abundance of marine resources.<ref name=pmid22194577/><ref>Boyd, I.L., Wanless, S. & Camphuysen, C.J. ====Popular====
Together with his father, [[John Morton Boyd]], he has written several books about the natural history of the Hebrides include one published in the [[Collins New Naturalist]] series.<ref>Boyd, J.M. & Boyd, I.L. (1990) The Hebrides. Collins (New Naturalist), 416pp.</ref>

====Policy====
In a 2017 article in the journal Science, "Toward pesticidovigilance", he called for a new approach to the regulation of pesticides<ref name=pmid28935789>{{cite journal |doi=10.1126/science.aan2683 |pmid=28935789 |title=Toward pesticidovigilance |journal=Science |volume=357 |issue=6357 |pages=1232–1234 |year=2017 |last1=Milner |first1=Alice M |last2=Boyd |first2=Ian L |bibcode=2017Sci...357.1232M |hdl=10023/13347 |s2cid=206659305 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/energy|title=Energy - Environment|website=The Guardian}}</ref> and he made further reference to pesticides in an explanation for the decision made by the UK government in April 2018 to support further restriction by the EU on [[neonicotinoid]] pesticides.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/s41559-018-0557-8 |pmid=29712984 |title=An Inside View on Pesticides Policy |journal=Nature Ecology and Evolution |volume=2 |issue=6 |pages=920–921 |last1=Boyd |first1=Ian L |year=2018|bibcode=2018NatEE...2..920B |hdl=10023/16352 |s2cid=14027049 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> He also published a recent article in Nature, "Taking the long view", which advocated taking a systems approach to understanding the problems which governments have to manage.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/540520a |pmid=30905962 |title=Take the long view |journal=Nature |volume=540 |issue=7634 |pages=520–521 |year=2016 |last1=Boyd |first1=Ian L |bibcode=2016Natur.540..520B |hdl=10023/13348 |s2cid=4446118 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

In 2015, he wrote an oped in [[The New York Times]] titled "Our deadened, carbon soaked seas"<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/10/16/opinion/our-deadened-carbon-soaked-seas.html|title=Opinion - Our Deadened, Carbon-Soaked Seas|first1=Richard W.|last1=Spinrad|first2=Ian|last2=Boyd|newspaper=The New York Times |date=15 October 2015}}</ref> with [[Rick Spinrad]] who was then the Chief Scientist at [[NOAA]] to draw attention to the dangers of ocean acidification. Also in 2015, he wrote an article on environmental forensics<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/506462/gs-15-37b-forensic-science-beyond-evidence.pdf |title=FORENSIC SCIENCE AND BEYOND|website=gov.uk |publisher=Government Office for Science }}</ref> where he said ''"We breathe, eat and drink other people's pollution. The 'tragedy of the commons' has a powerful presence across the environment. It has proved difficult to design market solutions to deal with these issues of equity."''

With co-author Sir [[Mark Walport]] he produced a report in 2017 on waste and resource productivity.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/from-waste-to-resource-productivity|title=From waste to resource productivity - GOV.UK}}</ref> When giving evidence to the UK Parliamentary [[Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Select Committee]] he said that it would be sensible to ''"bury plastic in landfill until science progresses"'' and that [[plastic waste]] should be stored in landfill sites until it can be mined.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.thetimes.com/article/bury-plastic-in-landfill-until-science-progresses-and-it-can-be-mined-says-ian-boyd-65slvsl2v|title=Bury plastic in landfill until science progresses|first=Ben Webster|last=Environment Editor|date=2 February 2018|via=www.thetimes.co.uk}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.parliamentlive.tv/Event/Index/9c6b4590-5882-4464-a945-29783d4af339|title=Parliamentlive.tv|website=www.parliamentlive.tv}}</ref> In 2018, also with Sir [[Mark Walport]], he co-edited a UK Government Foresight report<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/foresight-projects|title=Foresight Projects - GOV.UK|date=25 August 2023 }}</ref> on the Future of the Sea.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/future-of-the-sea--2|title=The Future of the Sea - GOV.UK}}</ref>

He has also provided commentary on the use of data in government saying ''"Across government there may be just about as many definitions of data as there are people"''.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/sdata.2017.131  |doi-access=free|pmid=28959451 |pmc=5604132 |title=The stuff and nonsense of open data in government |journal=Scientific Data |volume=4 |article-number=170131 |year=2017 |last1=Boyd |first1=Ian L |bibcode=2017NatSD...470131B }}</ref>

He also joined the UK's COVID-19 [[Scientific Advisory Group for Emergencies]] SAGE in late April 2020 and took part in its meetings until August 2021. In August 2022, he wrote an opinion piece in [[The Observer]] defending the way science advice was provided during the pandemic.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2022/aug/28/dont-blame-scientists-mr-sunak-when-governments-rarely-act-on-our-advice.html|title=Don't blame scientists, Mr Sunak, when government rarely act on our advice|first1=Ian|last1=Boyd|newspaper=The Observer |date=28 August 2022}}</ref>

In 2021, he became Co-Chair (with Scotland's First Minister) of the First Minister's Environment Council.

===Charity===
He is Chair of the [[UK Research Integrity Office]] and is a Trustee of the UK's [[National Oceanography Centre]] and the [[Campaign for Science and Engineering]]. He has been a member of the Council of Management of the Hebridean Trust for over 20 years. Until 2023, the trust owns the Treshnish Isleas in the Hebrides and has renovated the Skerryvore lighthouse supply station at [[Hynish]] on the island of Tiree to create an outdoor centre, holiday accommodation and affordable housing.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hebrideantrust.org/|title=HOME - The Hebridean Trust - conserving the historical and natural heritage of the Hebrides|website=www.hebrideantrust.org}}</ref>

===Controversy===
In July 2013, Boyd opined that ''"the scientific community needs to [be] avoiding suggesting that policies are either right or wrong; and being willing to make the voice of science heard by engaging with the mechanisms already available through science advisory committees, by working with embedded advisers (such as myself), and by being the voice of reason, rather than dissent, in the public arena."''<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.7554/eLife.01061 |pmid=23840934 |pmc=3699817 |title=Making science count in government |journal=eLife |volume=2 |article-number=e01061 |year=2013 |last1=Boyd |first1=Ian |doi-access=free }}</ref> The sentiment is seen as controversial by such people as [[Naomi Klein]]<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.newstatesman.com/2013/10/science-says-revolt|title=Naomi Klein: How science is telling us all to revolt|newspaper=New Statesman|date=10 June 2021 |last1=Klein |first1=Naomi }}</ref> and [[George Monbiot]], the latter of which described the opinion as ''"Shut up, speak through me, don't dissent – or your behaviour will ensure that science becomes irrelevant."''<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2013/sep/30/scientists-democracy-dissent-reasonable-boyd|title=For scientists in a democracy, to dissent is to be reasonable - George Monbiot|first=George|last=Monbiot|date=30 September 2013|website=The Guardian}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.taipeitimes.com/News/editorials/archives/2013/10/05/2003573745|title=Scientific reason is being replaced by political propaganda - Taipei Times|website=www.taipeitimes.com|date=5 October 2013 }}</ref>

In October 2013, Professor Boyd rebutted these opinions by Naomi Klein and George Monbiot.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2013/oct/06/scientists-speak-up-politicians-decide-policy|title=Scientists do speak up, but politicians decide policy - Ian Boyd|first=Ian|last=Boyd|date=6 October 2013|website=The Guardian}}</ref> Boyd stated that the point he was making in July was that ''"it is not their (scientists) job to make politicians' decisions for them – when scientists start providing opinions about whether policies are right or wrong they risk becoming politicised. A politicised scientist cannot also be an independent scientist."''

He was Chief Scientific Adviser at Defra through a period of controversy and change. Following the invasion of ash disease in to the UK in 2012, caused by the fungus ''[[Hymenoscyphus fraxineus]]'', he wrote a review of the effects of tree disease on ecosystems<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1126/science.1235773 |pmid=24233727 |title=The Consequence of Tree Pests and Diseases for Ecosystem Services |journal=Science |volume=342 |issue=6160 |article-number=1235773 |year=2013 |last1=Boyd |first1=I. L |last2=Freer-Smith |first2=P. H |last3=Gilligan |first3=C. A |last4=Godfray |first4=H. C. J |s2cid=27098882 }}</ref> and he also responded to criticism of some of Defra's methods used in badger culling.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/527038b |pmid=26536948 |title=DEFRA responds to badger-cull critique |journal=Nature |volume=527 |issue=7576 |page=38 |year=2015 |last1=Boyd |first1=Ian L |bibcode=2015Natur.527...38B |doi-access=free }}</ref> In 2013, he called for higher standards in policy-relevant science.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/501159a |pmid=24032133 |title=Research: A standard for policy-relevant science |journal=Nature |volume=501 |issue=7466 |pages=159–60 |year=2013 |last1=Boyd |first1=Ian |doi-access=free |bibcode=2013Natur.501..159B }}</ref>

In 2007 and 2008, he was Chief Scientist for the US Navy Behavioral Response Study which examined the responses of whales to naval anti-submarine sonar.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0017009 |pmid=21423729 |title=Beaked Whales Respond to Simulated and Actual Navy Sonar |journal=PLOS ONE |volume=6 |issue=3 |article-number=e17009 |year=2011 |last1=Tyack |first1=Peter L |last2=Zimmer |first2=Walter M. X |last3=Moretti |first3=David |last4=Southall |first4=Brandon L |last5=Claridge |first5=Diane E |last6=Durban |first6=John W |last7=Clark |first7=Christopher W |last8=d'Amico |first8=Angela |last9=Dimarzio |first9=Nancy |last10=Jarvis |first10=Susan |last11=McCarthy |first11=Elena |last12=Morrissey |first12=Ronald |last13=Ward |first13=Jessica |last14=Boyd |first14=Ian L |bibcode=2011PLoSO...617009T |pmc=3056662|doi-access=free }}</ref> This contributed to the case of [[Winter v. Natural Resources Defense Council]] in the [[US Supreme Court]].

==Honours and awards==
Boyd has received numerous honours and awards recognising his contributions to science, including the Scientific Medal of the [[Zoological Society of London]], the [[W. S. Bruce Medal]] for his research in Polar Science and has been elected as a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS), [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Edinburgh]] (FRSE) and is a [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Biology]] (FRSB).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gov.uk/government/people/ian-boyd|title=Professor Ian Boyd - GOV.UK|website=www.gov.uk}}</ref> He has held an honorary professorship at the University of Birmingham and was awarded the [[Antarctic Service Medal]] of the United States in 1995. In the same year he was awarded a [[Doctor of Science|DSc]] degree by the University of Aberdeen in 1995 for his research on mammalian physiological ecology. He led the Sea Mammal Research Unit at the University of St Andrews to the award of the [[Queen's Anniversary Prize]] in 2011. In 2017, he was awarded the [[Polar Medal]] and an honorary doctorate from the [[University of Exeter]] for his contribution to science and policy.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.exeter.ac.uk/honorarygraduates/2017/timetable/ceremony16/|title=Professor Ian L Boyd, BSc PhD DSc FSB FSRE - Honorary graduates - University of Exeter|website=www.exeter.ac.uk}}{{Dead link|date=March 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> He also has honorary doctorates from the [[University of Plymouth]], the [[University of Stirling]] and [[Heriot-Watt University]]. In 2021, he was awarded the Medal of the [[Chartered Institute of Ecology and Environmental Management]] (CIEEM).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://cieem.net/about-cieem/cieem-awards/cieem-medal/|title=Professor Ian L Boyd, BSc PhD DSc FSB FSRE FRS - 2021 Medal Winner|website=www.cieem.net}}</ref> In 2021, the [[University of St Andrews]] made him a Bishop Wardlaw Professor. In 2022, he received the Fletcher of Saltoun Award from the [[Saltire Society]] for his contribution to the cultural life of Scotland.

He was [[Knight Bachelor|knighted]] in the [[2019 Birthday Honours]] for services to science and economics on food and the environment.<ref>{{London Gazette|issue=62666|supp=y|page=B2|date=8 June 2019}}</ref>

==Personal life==
He married in 1982 and has one son and two daughters. He lives in [[London]], [[St Andrews]] and on the island of [[Tiree]] in the Hebrides.
